settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The code explicitly rejects any skip() result < 1 with `skipped < 1` throwing IOException, so the most common zero-return case is converted into an exception rather than an infinite loop.
For the common ByteArrayInputStream/FileInputStream sources used elsewhere in this library, skip() advances to the end and returns the number actually skipped, terminating the loop.
No caller of skipBytes was inspected in the read spans, so reachability with an adversarial stream is unproven.
candidates.description: BinaryFunctions.skipBytes(InputStream, long, String) loops `while (length != total)`, calling is.skip(length - total) and throwing only if the returned value is < 1. Some InputStream implementations (for example certain buffered/socket/network streams, or wrappers that return 0 when no bytes are immediately available without signalling EOF) can legitimately return 0 on a non-blocking-ish path, or return 0 repeatedly. In that case the condition `skipped < 1` would throw, so a plain 0 return is handled; however the function does not treat a 0-length skip as an EOF/error signal and there is no iteration cap, so any stream whose skip() blocks or otherwise never advances (while also never throwing and never returning < 1) would spin. The function is used by parsers to skip attacker-declared lengths, so a crafted file combined with a benign-looking stream behaviour could cause a CPU spin / denial of service. The negative case is also unhandled in principle for streams that return negative values other than -1 semantics, but the explicit `skipped < 1` check does reject negatives.
missing_evidence: Actual callers of skipBytes within the parsers and whether the length is attacker-controlled and unbounded.
Whether any supported ByteSource/InputStream implementation can return 0 from skip() without EOF in practice.
Presence/absence of an overall parsing timeout or size guard at the entry points (Imaging/ImageParser) outside the read spans.
preconditions: Caller invokes skipBytes with a length derived from untrusted image data (for example a skipped segment size).
The underlying InputStream's skip() returns 0 (or otherwise fails to advance) without throwing and without signalling EOF, repeatedly.
candidates.title: skipBytes can loop indefinitely when the stream repeatedly returns 0 from skip() without EOF

counter_evidence: readBytes throws IOException when the underlying stream reaches EOF before `length` bytes are read, so a length larger than the actual file still fails, albeit only after the oversized allocation attempt.
Many call sites elsewhere (not inspected here) may clamp or validate lengths before calling readBytes.
Java heap OOM from a single allocation is a resource-exhaustion concern, not memory corruption; exploitation requires the process to be memory-constrained or unguarded.
candidates.description: BinaryFunctions.readBytes(String, InputStream, int, String) performs `final byte[] result = new byte[length]` immediately, before any bytes are read. When a caller passes a length parsed from untrusted input (many image formats store segment/chunk/strip lengths as 16- or 32-bit native values), a hostile file can request a very large allocation and cause an OutOfMemoryError (heap exhaustion DoS) or, for a negative length derived from a signed interpretation, a NegativeArraySizeException that is not an ImageReadException and may escape the library's normal error contract. The helper itself performs no upper-bound check, no cross-check against remaining bytes available in the source, and does not degrade to streaming. The same pattern appears in the 3-arg overload and in readBytes(InputStream,int).
missing_evidence: Which callers pass unvalidated, attacker-controlled lengths to readBytes (e.g. chunk/segment/strip sizes) and whether any of them clamp the value first.
Whether entry points wrap parsing in try/catch for OutOfMemoryError or enforce a maximum input/length policy.
Whether negative lengths can actually reach readBytes given upstream type conversions.
preconditions: A format parser passes a length taken (directly or after arithmetic) from file data to readBytes.
The declared length is attacker-chosen and larger than available memory, or is negative due to signed interpretation of a crafted value.
candidates.title: readBytes allocates a byte array sized directly from an untrusted length before validating stream contents

counter_evidence: The comment block (lines 27-37) shows the authors were aware of format quirks around the leading 4 bytes, indicating some consideration of real-world inputs.

Upstream, IcnsDecoder (the caller) may validate that imageElement.data length is at least the expected size before invoking decompression; IcnsDecoder lines 1-200 do not perform that check for the 32-bpp path, but the remainder of IcnsDecoder and IcnsImageParser were not readable within the allowed spans.
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on malformed input is a robustness bug whose security impact (DoS vs. memory corruption) is limited in Java; no information disclosure is demonstrated.
candidates.description: Rle24Compression.decompress(width, height, data) computes `pixelCount = width * height` and allocates `result = new byte[4 * pixelCount]` using the dimensions supplied by the ICNS parsing layer. Inside the three-band loop the decoder advances a source index `dataPos` and a destination index `resultPos++` based purely on the run-length control bytes read from `data`, without checking that runs do not overrun either the source `data` array or the destination `result` array. Consequences that are plausible from this code alone: (1) if a run's `count` exceeds the remaining `pixelCount`, `result[band + 4*(resultPos++)]` indexes past the end of `result` producing an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; (2) `data[dataPos]` / `data[dataPos + 1]` can read past the end of the attacker-controlled `data` buffer; (3) if `width` and `height` are large and `width * height` overflows a signed int, `pixelCount` becomes negative or small and `new byte[4 * pixelCount]` yields a negative-size or wrongly-sized array. No width/height 0-or-negative check, no `pixelCount` overflow check, and no bounds guard on `dataPos`/`resultPos` exist in the method.
missing_evidence: The ICNS parsing layer (IcnsImageParser.readImageData/parse) that constructs the IcnsElement data array and how width/height are derived and validated.
Whether IcnsDecoder.decodeAllImages catches or lets AIOOBE/NegativeArraySizeException propagate before the image is used.
Confirmation of the maximum real-world width/height for the affected icns image types and whether int overflow is attainable.
preconditions: An attacker-supplied ICNS (or analogous container) element is routed through IcnsDecoder into Rle24Compression.decompress for a 32-bit-per-pixel image type.
The compressed element data is such that a run length drives resultPos beyond pixelCount, or dataPos beyond data.length, or the declared width*height overflows int.
candidates.title: ICNS RLE decompression writes into a fixed-size result buffer without validating per-run or source-length bounds

counter_evidence: The 1-bpp mask path does contain a length check (lines 157-162), so not every path is unguarded.
IcnsImageParser (the caller, outside the readable spans) may validate element data length against the expected uncompressed size before calling these decoders.
The impact observed here would be a runtime exception on malformed input rather than a proven memory-safety or disclosure issue in Java.
candidates.description: IcnsDecoder contains several decoders that iterate over imageType.getWidth()/getHeight() and index a caller-supplied byte[] imageData directly, with no check that imageData is large enough for the declared dimensions: decode1BPPImage (imageData[position++]), decode4BPPImage (imageData[i] / imageData[i++]), decode8BPPImage (imageData[y*width + x]) and decode32BPPImage (imageData[4*(y*width + x) + 1..3]). Likewise the mask helpers apply1BPPMask (maskData[position++]) and apply8BPPMask (maskData[y*width + x]) index attacker-controlled mask buffers. For a crafted ICNS whose element data is shorter than the geometry implies, these produce ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (and, for 32-bpp, multiplications that can overflow int before indexing). apply1BPPMask does perform a partial size check (encoding comment at lines 155-157, comparing maskData.length to `(width*height+7)/8` and throwing '1 BPP mask underrun parsing ICNS file' when maskData.length < 2*totalBytes), showing the library knows to guard one case but the other decoders have no equivalent guard within the read span.
missing_evidence: The IcnsImageParser code that reads element lengths and decides how much data to pass to IcnsDecoder (not in the readable spans).
Whether decode1/4/8/32BPP are reachable with mismatched data length in practice, and whether exceptions are handled or propagated to the application.
Any global catch of ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at the Imaging entry points.
preconditions: A crafted ICNS file declares image element types whose dimensions exceed the actual element payload length.
The element is routed through IcnsDecoder.decodeAllImages into one of the unguarded decoders (1/4/8/32 bpp or the 8bpp mask path).
candidates.title: ICNS fixed-palette decoders index arrays using dimensions and pixel data with no length validation

counter_evidence: maven.compiler.source/target are bytecode/source level hints; consumers may run on a newer supported JVM even if the artifact targets 1.7.

pom.xml lines 1-80 show only the project description/properties/scm/distribution/issue sections; the dependency and plugin management sections (lines 81-471) were not read, so central security-relevant configuration may exist there.
This is a hygiene/finding-level observation, not a demonstrated exploitable vulnerability.
candidates.description: pom.xml sets maven.compiler.source/target to 1.7 (lines 47-48) and uses commons-parent 47 (line 29) with version 1.0-SNAPSHOT (line 36). Building and shipping artifacts against an end-of-life language/VM baseline means the library is compiled for a platform that no longer receives security updates, and the parent/plugin versions are inherited without explicit security-relevant pinning in the visible portion of the POM. The visible properties also set a fixed -Xmx512m test JVM (line 46), which constrains the heap for tests but does not impose any runtime limit on library consumers.
missing_evidence: The remainder of pom.xml (dependencyManagement, dependencies, plugin configuration, any enforcer/OWASP dependency-check plugin) which was outside the readable span.
The effective configuration inherited from commons-parent 47, not present in this repository.
Whether the project actually releases 1.7-targeted bytecode or documents minimum supported runtime.
preconditions: The library is built and distributed using this POM as-is to a JVM/platform baseline that includes the deprecated Java 7 target semantics.
candidates.title: build configuration targets an obsolete Java version and lacks any dependency/plugin pinning for security tooling
